response.consequence: A timing side channel on the shared secret is possible in principle. It is hard to exploit over a network, which is why this is low severity. Authenticated callers who send malformed input get an unhandled 500.
response.explanation: The handler compares the request header to process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET with `!==`, which is not constant-time. The unset-secret bypass in the hypothesis does not occur. response.consequence: With credential sync enabled, the first refresh corrupts the saved refresh_token in the database. Later refreshes fail because the refresh token is invalid. The expiry is never updated, so every call triggers a refresh. Integrations that persist the parsed data, such as Office365, are affected.
response.explanation: The two computed keys, z.string().toString() and z.string().optional().toString(), both evaluate to the same constant, "[object Object]". Zod does not override toString. The second key overwrites the first, so the schema is really {access_token: string, "[object Object]": unknown.optional()}. The "any number property is the expiry" rule is never enforced. The default z.object strips unknown keys, so the parsed data holds only access_token. It loses expiry_date, expires_in, refresh_token and any other fields. The hypothesis that safeParse always fails is wrong. The schema accepts any object with a string access_token, but it drops everything else. parseRefreshTokenResponse then sets data.refresh_token to the literal "refresh_token" because the stripped data never has one. Callers merge this data into the stored credential. For example, office365calendar/lib/CalendarService.ts:264 spreads tokenResponse.data over o365AuthCredentials and saves it with prisma.credential.update. That overwrites the real stored refresh_token with the string "refresh_token". The new expiry is never stored, so the stale expiry stays.
response.title: Credential-sync token schema is degenerate and placeholder refresh_token overwrites stored credentials

response.consequence: After the first access-token refresh, a user's Google Calendar credential is overwritten with a malformed key. Every later use of that credential fails, and the user has to reconnect.
response.explanation: parseRefreshTokenResponse returns the zod safeParse result, which has the shape {success, data}. It does not return the parsed data. The old code stored `googleCredentialSchema.parse(googleCredentials)`, which was the credential itself. The new code assigns the wrapper to `key` and passes it to prisma.credential.update. After the first token refresh, the stored key is {success: true, data: {...}}. It no longer has access_token, refresh_token or expiry_date at the top level. The next `googleCredentialSchema.parse(credential.key)` in googleAuth then throws.

response.explanation: The computed keys `[z.string().toString()]` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]` both evaluate to the literal string "[object Object]", not a wildcard.
